Apologies for the late reply. I've been on vacation and trying to crawl out of my inbox ever since.

Also, thanks for working on this. This would certainly be an improvement to move that processing to HTML, and will make it more coherent and up to date (e.g. handling of integrity, nonces and referrerpolicy were neglected on preload's end :/).

The current change doesn't seem sufficient when compared with preload's "obtain" section:
* Preload's processing validates the `as` attribute as a valid destination, and if it's not, the resource fetch is aborted. It also triggers an error event in that case.
* Unsupported MIME type in `type` and non-matching MQ in `media` result in a silent abort of the fetch.

Can you add those parts as well?

> Preload's processing validates the as attribute as a valid destination, and if it's not, the resource fetch is aborted. It also triggers an error event in that case.

This is actually not possible given the processing model of enumerated attributes. Enumerated attributes always have an "invalid value default", in this case the empty string (signaling a fetch destination). So it wasn't possible to implement the processing model of validating and giving an error.

> Unsupported MIME type in type and non-matching MQ in media result in a silent abort of the fetch.

These are already accounted for because the fetch won't even be started in that case: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#processing-the-media-attribute and https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#processing-the-type-attribute

> This is actually not possible given the processing model of enumerated attributes. Enumerated attributes always have an "invalid value default", in this case the empty string (signaling a fetch destination). So it wasn't possible to implement the processing model of validating and giving an error.

That part is critical for future proofing preload. UAs need to trigger an error when an invalid `as` value is encountered, as it may signify a not-yet-support destination, and Web developers would need a way to know that it is not supported and potentially load it differently. If we cannot do that, we might need to split the 1:1 relationship between `as` values and destination (which we might have to do anyway for https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/pull/442)

Oh, this is indeed very problematic; I'm surprised nobody caught it earlier. It seems like preload perhaps shouldn't even be a link relation or HTML element at all, if it can't follow normal HTML element rules.
Note that error events do not get fired for Link headers, further indicating that the `<link>` element might not be a good choice here.
Can you provide some code that would "load it differently" but not also run into this problem?

> Note that error events do not get fired for Link headers, further indicating that the <link> element might not be a good choice here.

That doesn't seem to be true for Chrome, Safari or Firefox when presented with a 404ed stylesheet ([Test case](http://jsbin.com/heyakumomu/edit?html,output))



> Can you provide some code that would "load it differently" but not also run into this problem?
>  Show all reviewers

The use case I have in mind for that is something like [markup based async loader](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2016/02/preload-what-is-it-good-for/#markup-based-async-loader) where developers use preload to simply load the resource and rely on its `onload` event to use it when it's ready. Knowing it is not supported would enable them to e.g. include it in another markup form or load it using `fetch()`.
@yoavweiss that's not using a `Link` HTTP header though.

> @yoavweiss that's not using a Link HTTP header though.

Apologies, I totally misread @domenic's comment, and missed the "header" part. Yeah, headers don't have error events (nor load events), so cannot be used for such loading patterns that require feature detection.

> Knowing it is not supported would enable them to e.g. include it in another markup form or load it using fetch().

But those will suffer from the same problem: without support for that request destination, they will not end up in the preload cache. So I still don't see how this feature is necessary.

> But those will suffer from the same problem: without support for that request destination, they will not end up in the preload cache. So I still don't see how this feature is necessary.

My use of "invalid" was wrong. The destination won't be invalid (it would be defined by the spec at that point), but may not be supported for preload (like the way that currently "document" is a valid destination but is not a supported for preload in implementations). 

But since we're not talking about an invalid destination, that might make things simpler. Can we add a condition indicating that processing should be aborted if `rel` is `preload` and `as` contains a destination that is not supported for preload by the UA?

I'm still confused. In this hypothetical code that falls back to fetch(), it still doesn't end up in the preload cache, since by assumption the browser does not have a preload cache for the given destination. So what was the point of the fallback at all?

I'd really like to understand what use case we're addressing before we add extra complexity to address it.

Let me try to explain myself better.
Let's consider iframe preloading or `as=document`. Currently it is not supported in implementations for various reasons, but is defined as a valid destination.
Let's say that in the future some browsers supported `document` preloading, while others don't.
A developer may want to preload a certain iframe while avoiding the side-effects of creating an `<iframe>` node early (delays to `window.onload`, etc). 

In that case, they can add a `<link rel=preload href="iframe.html" onload="use_iframe('iframe.html')" onerror="fallback('iframe.html')">` where `fallback()` simply creates the iframe node and adds to the DOM and suffers the side-effects. That would mean that preload supporting browsers would have a better loading experience, but the iframe would still work even if preloading of that destination is not supported.

I hope that is clearer. Let me know if further clarifications are required.

Also, this is where we originally added that logic: https://github.com/w3c/preload/issues/36#issuecomment-185270277

/cc @igrigorik

Sorry, I'm still confused. Simply creating an iframe node *still doesn't add iframe.html to the preload cache*, since *by assumption*, there is no preload cache for iframes in this browser. So what does this actually accomplish? What is the "better loading experience", concretely? Is it about it being in the HTTP cache, for example?

Here's another point of my confusion, from https://github.com/w3c/preload/issues/36#issuecomment-185270277:

> That can cause a situation where introducing browser support to a new destination value can result in double downloads in non-supporting browsers (which fetch the preload resource as an empty destination, which means it will not match any resource that is not an empty destination, e.g XHR).

This doesn't seem true. For example, in a browser that does not support as="document", under this PR it will fetch with the empty destination. But since the browser doesn't support as="document", it doesn't have a preload or memory cache for documents; it will just use the normal non-specific cache. Which means that when we later see `<iframe src="iframe.html"></iframe>`, it will just continue to use the normal non-specific cache. There's no double-request there; it uses the cache as expected.

Stated another way, the idea that fetches with empty-string destination will not match iframes is false. If the browser doesn't implement a special destiniation for iframes, then fetches with empty-string destination are exactly what iframes match, since they don't have anything more specific to match.

> For example, in a browser that does not support as="document", under this PR it will fetch with the empty destination. But since the browser doesn't support as="document", it doesn't have a preload or memory cache for documents; it will just use the normal HTTP cache. Which means that when we later see <iframe src="iframe.html"></iframe>, it will just continue to use the normal HTTP cache. There's no double-request there; it uses the cache as expected.

That assumes that the resource in question is cacheable. At least for iframes, that's a far-fetched assumption, which will often result in a double download.
Sure, that's why I edited my post to "normal non-specific cache" (i.e. the preload empty-string-destination cache) instead of "normal HTTP cache".

> Sure, that's why I edited my post to "normal non-specific cache" (i.e. the preload empty-string-destination cache) instead of "normal HTTP cache".

Heh, that edit did not auto-update for me :)

Unfortunately, that won't work. If the destination does not match, the preload cache won't be able to serve that resource as it may break CSP correctness (`document` may have different/tighter restrictions than the empty destination). Otherwise there may be other correctness issues with serving resources with a destination mismatch.

_Aside 1_: The preload cache is not yet defined. We totally should define it.
_Aside 2_: My comments above are doubly true today when the preload cache is implemented by the MemoryCache (Although it may [soon](https://codereview.chromium.org/2871233002/) be easier to separate MemoryCache matching logic from the preload cache)

So @ddragana ran into one of the issues discussed here. Namely that we have tests that expect `as="invalidvalue"` to normalize to the empty string, just like omitting the `as` attribute normalizes to the empty string, but then we also have tests (`preload/download-resources.html` in WPT) that expect those two cases to have different behavior (invalid values don't download, valid values do). That seems like a really strange API and not at all well defined.

> Namely that we have tests that expect as="invalidvalue" to normalize to the empty string

Why do we have such tests? What spec are they based on?
@yoavweiss https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics.html#dom-link-as.

I did not think that the fact that `as` is reflected as an empty string means that it should be processed as one. If that's the case, maybe it should not be "reflected and limited only to known values".

I could be convinced that we can replace the "onerror" based fallback with "reflect only known values" feature detection. But avoiding actually sending the request when the `as` value is unknown is critical to avoid double downloads.

You could have a different fallback for invalid values maybe. Not sure if anything does that, but it sure does like HTML provides  the necessary means for it.

(It also doesn't necessarily mean you need to process it as such, but it sure would make sense if how `as` got reflected actually aligns with the processing model, so you need a single data structure to implement things.)

So maybe a way forward is:
* `as` stays as defined right now - "reflected & limited to known values". That's fine as we want to eliminate loading of empty `as` values anyway in https://github.com/w3c/preload/issues/80#issuecomment-268573775.
* `as` will be mapped to "potential destination" as discussed in https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/pull/442#discussion_r103624566 which will not support the empty value, and avoid loading of such resources.
* Feature detection of supported preload `as` values would be based on the reflected value.

@igrigorik - thoughts on the switch from `onerror` based fallback to feature detection?
That sounds good to me. Chromium shipping that model quickly would help in getting Firefox to adopt it.

> @igrigorik - thoughts on the switch from onerror based fallback to feature detection?

Not sure I follow.. Here's what we recommended before: https://gist.github.com/igrigorik/a02f2359f3bc50ca7a9c. How is the new proposal different?

Also, if we're considering changing processing requirements for empty `as`.. Do we have a sense for impact on existing usage?
@igrigorik that detects "preload" support, it doesn't detect support for an `as` attribute value.
@annevk right, gotcha. @yoavweiss gave me a quick tl;dr... this all looks good!
Related: https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/pull/547 was merged and https://codereview.chromium.org/2903653005 implements the discussed changes for Chromium and adds WPT tests.
@annevk - PRed at https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/pull/549

Added the required changes here (I think) to https://github.com/yoavweiss/html/commit/ed99510d897c7dafacce537d177ee4b1cfc7b90d

@domenic - I'm not sure if I should PR those changes separately, or if they should be merged into this PR. Let me know which is preferred.

Interesting, so "" is a potential destination too. But I guess if someone says as="" (or omits the as attribute entirely) we want to abort the request? That's not what your patch does, since "" is a valid potential destination, but I have a fix incoming for you to review...

> Interesting, so "" is a potential destination too.

That's a mistake... https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/pull/549 fixes it. Can you perhaps review that in @annevk's absence?
Ah yep, will merge, and then tomorrow will update this PR to have fewer workarounds for that.

@yoavweiss this should be ready for review. I've also updated the reflection web platform tests at https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2588. For the Chromium intent-to-ship, I assume you are also writing some web platform tests on the actual processing, not just the reflection?

> For the Chromium intent-to-ship, I assume you are also writing some web platform tests on the actual processing, not just the reflection?

Yeah, the tests that are part of https://codereview.chromium.org/2903653005/ test the processing changes (and specifically, the fact that onerror doesn't fire for invalid `as`, including an empty one, and that `as=fetch` replaces a missing `as` or an empty one)

I found as="fetch" confusing.

Reading https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#miscellaneous, concrete sentence:
"If potentialDestination is "fetch", then return the empty string. "
I understand that "fetch" will map to empty string:
```
var link = document.createElement("link");
link.as = "fetch";
assert_true(link.as == "");
```

Anther person read paragraph  https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-potential-destination and understood that:
`assert_true(link.as == "fetch");`
Why do you think the translate algorithm is called when triggering the `.as` getter? There is nothing in the spec that indicates so.
Ok, I misunderstood it.
